title: Motzkin-Straus Optimization on an Entropy-Computing Platform
authors: PoJen Wang, Sutapa Samanta, Yuntai Song, Mohammad-Ali Miri
abstract: We introduce a framework for combinatorial optimization using sum-constrained continuous quadratic programs solvable by QCi's Dirac-3S photonic entropy computer. This is enabled by the Motzkin-Straus theorem which provides a powerful bridge between discrete clique problems and optimization over the probability simplex. We demonstrate this framework's versatility by solving constraint satisfaction problems, providing extensive benchmarks on the DIMACS suite. The Dirac-3S platform matches or outright leads two independently implemented classical baselines on more than four-fifths of the benchmark instances, reaching the best known solution on nearly all structured graph families, even outperforming both classical solvers on several of the largest instances tested. On the other hand, well-tuned classical continuous optimizers retain an edge only on the hardest planted-clique instances. This work establishes a viable pathway for solving combinatorial optimization problems using natively analog unconventional computing platforms, while positioning entropy computing as a competitive approach for navigating non-convex landscapes and providing rigorous baselines for an emerging computational paradigm.
summary: This paper introduces a method to solve hard combinatorial optimization problems, like finding the maximum clique, by reformulating them as continuous quadratic programs solvable on a photonic entropy computer. The authors benchmark this platform against leading classical solvers, showing it is highly competitive and establishes entropy computing as a promising new paradigm for tackling classically intractable problems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the NP-hard problem of finding the maximum clique (or maximum independent set) in a graph.
main_result: The proposed entropy computing platform (Dirac-3S) demonstrates performance matching or exceeding state-of-the-art classical solvers on most benchmark instances.
method: It reformulates the discrete clique problem into a continuous quadratic program solvable via the Motzkin-Straus theorem, which is then implemented on the photonic entropy computer.
model_or_system: The core system is the Dirac-3S photonic entropy computer, which solves the quadratic program subject to probability simplex constraints using photon number encoding. The problem is mathematically mapped to minimizing a quadratic form over the probability simplex.
key_observables: The primary observable is the size of the maximum clique, $\omega(G)$, derived from the minimum energy $f^*$ found by the optimization process.
important_parameters: The scaling parameter $R$ for the probability simplex, and the number of restarts/initializations used in classical benchmarking.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that solving the continuous quadratic program on the entropy computer provides a viable pathway to the discrete optimal solution, although extraction methods (rounding, support-based) are necessary.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mapping from the Max Clique problem to a quadratic optimization problem and show the entropy computing architecture using photon number encoding.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the framework, details the Motzkin-Straus mapping, presents the Dirac-3S platform's implementation, benchmarks its performance against classical solvers (Armijo-PGD, Hexaly) on DIMACS suites, and concludes by establishing the viability of entropy computing for combinatorial optimization.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the computational bottleneck of NP-hard problems by proposing a novel, hardware-native approach (entropy computing) that bypasses traditional quantum circuit overheads, making it highly relevant to quantum computation paradigms.

Fig. 2 Summary of solver performance on the 75 DIMACS benchmark graphs. For each solver, the bars show the number of instances on which it (i) matches best known, i.e. returns a clique size equal to the best known value (or best known lower bound) in Table 1; (ii) is the strict best of three, i.e. returns a clique strictly larger than those of both other solvers; and (iii) is best or tied, i.e. returns a clique at least as large as those of both other solvers, including ties. The counts in each category are taken directly from Table 1.
